Freelance engineering vs permanent: what changes

For experienced engineers in Italy and Spain: what working as a freelancer with a partita IVA or as an autónomo really involves, and when it pays off.

  1. Home
  2. Insights
  3. Freelance engineering vs permanent: what changes

24 November 2026 · 5 min read

  • Article
  • Experienced engineers

At some point most experienced engineers wonder whether to go freelance. More control over the projects you take, a higher daily rate, no annual review. It can be a great move. It is also a different job: alongside the engineering, you run a small business.

This article explains what changes when you work on projects as an independent professional in Italy or Spain, and how to tell whether it suits you. It is not tax or legal advice: rules change, and an accountant who knows your situation is worth their fee from day one.

What changes on day one

As an employee, your employer handles most of the paperwork. As a freelancer, it is yours:

  • You invoice your clients and wait for payment on the agreed terms.
  • You pay your own taxes and social security contributions, on dates set by law, from the money you have invoiced.
  • Nobody pays you for holidays, sick days or the weeks between projects. Your rate has to cover them.
  • Training, equipment and insurance are your costs. So is your accountant.
  • You set your rate and negotiate your contracts. Nobody negotiates a pay rise for you.

In return, you choose your projects and clients, decide how you organise your work, and can grow your income by managing your rate and your time well.

Italy: working with a partita IVA

In Italy, you open a VAT number (partita IVA) with the tax agency and choose a tax regime. Many people starting out use the simplified flat-rate regime (regime forfettario) if they meet its conditions; others use the ordinary regime. The thresholds and rates change, so check the current rules with a commercialista before you decide.

Your pension contributions depend on your activity. Engineers enrolled in the professional register who carry out engineering work usually contribute to the profession’s own fund; many other technical freelancers contribute to the INPS separate scheme (gestione separata). Your accountant will tell you which applies to you.

Spain: working as an autónomo

In Spain, you register with the tax agency and with the social security scheme for the self-employed (RETA). Since 2023, your monthly contribution depends on your expected net income, and is adjusted once your actual income is known. You file VAT and income tax returns every quarter, which is why most autónomos work with a gestor or an accountant.

If most of your income comes from a single client, Spanish law has a specific status for economically dependent self-employed workers (TRADE), with its own rights and obligations. Ask your adviser whether it applies to you.

Independence is a legal matter

In both countries, being a freelancer is not just a label on the contract. It depends on how the work is actually done. A genuine independent professional:

  • delivers an agreed scope, with deliverables and a duration;
  • decides how to organise the work, within what the project needs;
  • uses their own tools and can work for other clients;
  • is paid for the work, not for being available for a set number of hours.

If a “freelance” role looks exactly like a full-time job, with fixed hours, a line manager and no defined deliverables, be careful. Both Italy and Spain treat disguised employment seriously, and the risk is not only the client’s: you lose the protections of an employee without gaining the freedom of a freelancer.

How to think about your rate

The most common mistake is to divide a salary by the working days in a year. Your rate has to cover much more:

  • the days you won’t bill: holidays, illness, training, and the gaps between projects;
  • your taxes and social security contributions;
  • your accountant, insurance, equipment and software;
  • the protections you give up, such as paid leave and severance.

Compare your expected net income with the full value of a permanent package, not just the gross salary, and make the comparison with your accountant’s help.

When permanent makes more sense

  • You want to grow into a leadership role inside one organisation.
  • You value stability, paid leave and a predictable income.
  • You are moving into a new discipline and want to learn from a team over several years.
  • You would rather spend your time on engineering than on invoices, contracts and finding the next project.

When freelance makes more sense

  • You have deep, in-demand expertise that companies need for specific projects or phases.
  • You enjoy variety, new teams and new problems.
  • You have a network, or a partner, who can help you find the next project.
  • You have savings to cover a gap between projects without stress.

Questions to ask before you accept a project

  • What exactly is the scope, and what are the deliverables?
  • How long is the project, and what happens if the scope changes?
  • What is the rate, and what are the payment terms?
  • On site, hybrid or remote? Who pays for travel?
  • Who owns the work you produce?
  • How can either side end the contract early?
  • Do you need professional liability insurance for this work?

If the answers are vague, ask again before you sign. A well-run project starts with a clear contract.

How we work with freelancers

Through our temporary staffing service, we introduce independent engineers and technical consultants to companies for specific projects. Scope, duration and rate are agreed clearly before the project starts, under a project or consulting contract, and we never share your CV without your OK.
